extracted.intended_audience: educated readers and students of natural philosophy, geology, biology, and social theory (Victorian-era readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A philosophical/scientific essay arguing a general law of progress: that single forces produce multiple effects which drive the transformation from homogeneity to heterogeneity across inorganic, chemical, organic, and social domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every active force produces more than one change
rubrics_metrics.description: The fundamental law asserted: a single active force, when expended, produces multiple distinct effects rather than a single change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as a universal principle and illustrated throughout the text (geological, chemical, organic, social examples). The author emphasizes that this multiplicity of effects is the key mechanism by which systems evolve from homogeneous to heterogeneous states. Also noted as holding when a force is withdrawn (the withdrawal of a force produces more than one change).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heterogeneity of effects increases with heterogeneity of the object
rubrics_metrics.description: In proportion to the heterogeneity of the object(s) on which a force expends itself, is the heterogeneity of the effects produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained using geological examples: a complex continent exposing many strata under denuding agencies yields innumerable and involved results; conversely, a tolerably even surface raised from the sea has a simple sea-margin. Use this as a predictive criterion: more complex initial structure → more diverse outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crustal contraction and cooling produce increasing geological heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: As the Earth's solid envelope grew thicker and cooled, contraction caused increased elevation differences, more irregular coast-lines, and a transition from homogenously dispersed islands to heterogeneous arrangements of continent and ocean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with the orange-and-paper thought experiment: thin vs thick wrapping produces different wrinkle heights and spacing. Use this to connect thermal contraction to progressive geological complexity (mountain chains, table-lands, irregular outlines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Denuding (aqueous and atmospheric) agencies multiply and vary surface changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents like oxidation, heat, wind, frost, rain, glaciers, rivers, tides, and waves continuously produce disintegration and differing effects according to local circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples: acting on granite vs feldspar-bearing rocks yields very different outcomes (exfoliation and boulders vs decomposition into clay and separate bed deposition). Different rivers carry different detritus leading to new, unlike strata. Use to assess how surface processes generate heterogeneous results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound causes dominate natural change; single-cause attributions are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Most changes are produced by compound sets of concurrent causes (e.g., cooling of Earth plus aqueous/atmospheric agencies plus affinities of elements); attributing change to one agency alone risks inaccuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author prefers popular single-cause phrasing for simplicity but warns that practically every change depends on multiple temporary or permanent conditions. Also addresses the linguistic inaccuracy of saying 'loss of heat' causes freezing, clarifying that forces acting when antagonistic forces are withdrawn produce effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical heterogeneity increases as temperature falls; stability decreases with complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: As Earth cooled, the first chemical compounds formed were the simplest and most stable (protoxides); progressively more complex compounds (deutoxides, tritoxides, hydrates, salts, hydrated salts, supersalts) appeared later and are generally less stable. Organic compounds show still greater complexity and lower stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the sequence and examples given (protoxides → deutoxides/tritoxides → hydrates → salts → hydrated salts → supersalts) and the empirical claim 'other things equal, the stability decreases as the complexity increases.' Examples include albumen and fibrine molecular complexity and their instability at ordinary temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single force acting on a complicated area produces enormously ramified, long-range consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale disturbances (e.g., subsidence of Central America) produce immediate complex local effects (earthquakes, eruptions, waves) and permanent global effects (altered ocean currents, changed isothermal lines, modified tides and winds, widespread meteorological and ecological revolutions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion for judging systemic impact: assess both immediate local dislocations and longer-term, far-reaching alterations in climate, currents, and biota. The text emphasizes that temporary effects pale compared to permanent reorganizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication of effects explains organic development from germ to organism
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryonic development proceeds by repeated actions of incident forces on the existing partial organization, each change superinducing further complications until increasing complexities produce the mature organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument supported by cell-division observations: the early embryo produces a mass of undifferentiated cells, and successive interactions among developing parts (heart pulsations, tissue growth altering blood constitution, nervous connections) initiate further differentiations. This frames development as an iterative cascade of effects rather than a single directing cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental variation and dispersal cause divergence and multiplication of species/varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: When regions change (e.g., uplift of archipelagos into continents), species exposed to slightly different climates, levels, foods, and habits diverge into many varieties or new species; dispersion increases survival chances and yields both upward and downward (retrograde) changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated with the East Indian Archipelago example: different members of species experience different conditions (coast vs mountains, equator vs away), producing multiple radiating forms from an original race. Also notes that sometimes simpler habits cause retrogression, so divergence is not uniformly progressive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes of habit and interspecific contact produce further organic modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: New habits prompted by encountering unfamiliar species (predators/prey) or altered food resources can lead to behavioral changes that, if dominant, alter organization and contribute to differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as criterion: consider both physical/environmental causes and behavioral shifts as proximate causes of morphological/physiological change (examples include herbivores adapting defenses, and bee larva developing into queen with changed diet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social heterogeneity arises from individual specialization and division of labor
rubrics_metrics.description: When some individuals show aptitude for particular tasks (e.g., a weapon-maker), a division of labor emerges (barter, specialization), producing social differentiation and many secondary effects (new occupations, intensified skill, changed production processes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weapon-maker example traces mechanism: skill + client demand → specialization; barter spreads specialization; increased demand and population pressure intensify specialization, leading to new occupations and further social complexity. Use this to analyze sociocultural evolution driven by functional differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological innovations have multifold, ramifying consequences across material, intellectual, and moral domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions and material substitutions (bronze for stone, steam power, the locomotive, printing, gunpowder) set off cascades of changes affecting manufacture, processes, buildings, tastes, comfort, trade patterns, and habits of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: bronze changes manufacturing and makes possible new articles; steam and railways change the face of the country, trade, and habits; printing and gunpowder produce multitudinous material, intellectual, and moral effects. Use to evaluate the systemic impact of a technology beyond its immediate utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of forms proceeds by continual divergence (branching), not linear serial substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The succession of organic forms is not merely serial replacement but occurs by perpetual divergence and re-divergence — a 'divergence of many races from one race', with each species as a 'root' giving rise to multiple descendant forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented in a footnote clarifying the author's historical stance and noting compatibility (in part) with later ideas of natural selection; the tree metaphor is invoked as the implied symbol. Use this as a model for interpreting phylogenetic patterns as branching rather than linear progress.
